paper_title: Methodologies for Developing Consumption-Based Urban GHG Emission Inventories: A Systematic Review
paper_abstract: As cities emerge as the primary drivers of global consumption-based emissions, the need for greenhouse gas (GHG) accounting methods that model multisectoral urban interactions has become paramount. In this context, consumption-based (CB) urban GHG emission inventories have arisen as a useful tool for political decision-makers. This systematic literature review was carried out across three databases, covering al-most 20 years of publications strictly related to the elaboration of CB GHG emission inventories, reaching a total of 100 publications. More than a third of the articles ex-plored Life-Cycle Assessment (LCA), 34% used Environmentally-Extended In-put-Output Analysis (EEIOA), with only 10% delving into hybrid methodologies. A case study comparison was performed for cities that applied different methodologies, in terms of carbon footprint. The strengths and weaknesses of each framework were also assessed. The results showed that both EEIOA and LCA were useful to model complex carbon flows and accounted for the majority of emissions associated to urban activity. EEIOA excelled for its operational simplicity and speed in the calculation of carbon footprint when input-output matrices are available, but it was not as suitable for policy-making. LCA required a larger volume of information and its processing was more time-consuming, but it was also capable of identifying hotspots. Hybrid approaches obtained carbon footprint results similar to those of EEIOA or LCA, while covering certain weaknesses of these standalone methodologies.

paper_title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism Beyond Calcium: FGF23 Dynamics After Parathyroidectomy and the Unresolved Postoperative PTH Phenotype—A Narrative Review
paper_abstract: Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) is definitively treated by parathyroidectomy (PTx), with surgical cure conventionally defined by sustained normocalcemia. However, some patients develop elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) concentrations despite normal postoperative calcium levels. This heterogeneous condition may reflect vitamin D insufficiency, reduced calcium availability, skeletal remineralization, or renal dysfunction, but may occasionally indicate persistent parathyroid autonomy or precede biochemical recurrence. Fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), an osteocyte-derived regulator of phosphate excretion and calcitriol synthesis, occupies a central position within the bone–kidney–parathyroid axis and may participate in metabolic adaptation after PTx. This narrative review examines FGF23 regulation, circulating concentrations, clinical associations, and perioperative dynamics in PHPT. A structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science identified 11 original clinical studies directly evaluating FGF23 in PHPT. Findings were discordant: some studies reported increased preoperative concentrations and a postoperative decline, whereas others found normal levels or no significant change after surgery. Differences in disease phenotype, renal function, vitamin D status, assay methodology, supplementation, and sampling time may partly explain this heterogeneity. Notably, no study related perioperative FGF23 changes to subsequent PTH trajectories, and studies of postoperative eucalcemic PTH elevation did not measure FGF23. FGF23 cannot currently be considered a diagnostic or prognostic biomarker in PHPT. Nevertheless, serial assessment alongside conventional mineral-metabolism parameters may clarify endocrine adaptation after PTx and determine whether biologically distinct postoperative phenotypes exist.

paper_title: Optimizing Malaria and Communicable Disease Interventions: A Comprehensive Review of Mathematical Models to Control Malaria
paper_abstract: Malaria remains a major global public health challenge, with a substantial burden of morbidity and mortality concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa and other tropical and subtropical regions. The complex transmission process involving Plasmodium parasites, Anopheles mosquito vectors, and human hosts makes mathematical modeling an important tool for understanding transmission dynamics and evaluating control strategies. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of mathematical modeling approaches for malaria transmission and control, including deterministic compartmental models, stochastic models, optimal control frameworks, spatial models, and cost-effectiveness analyses. Particular attention is given to major intervention strategies, including vector control, vaccination, antimalarial treatment, and other integrated control approaches. The review also examines the effects of seasonality, climate variability, drug and insecticide resistance, spatial heterogeneity, and human movement on malaria transmission and intervention outcomes. A bibliography-based keyword frequency analysis and word-cloud visualization are used to identify dominant research themes, followed by a comparative assessment of modeling approaches and intervention strategies. The findings highlight the importance of integrating multiple interventions with context-specific epidemiological and environmental conditions. Overall, mathematical models provide valuable support for optimizing malaria control strategies and addressing important challenges toward malaria elimination.

paper_title: Social Relationships, Depressive Symptoms, and Self-Rated Health Among Adults Living Alone in South Korea: An Analysis of the 2025 Korea Community Health Survey
paper_abstract: This study examined associations between social relationships, depressive symptoms, and self-rated health (SRH) among adults living alone in South Korea. Data from 44,168 adults living alone who participated in the 2025 Korea Community Health Survey were analyzed using complex-samples logistic regression. Social relationships included contact frequency with family members or relatives, neighbors, and friends and neighborhood trust. Depressive symptoms were defined as a Patient Health Questionnaire-9 score ≥ 10. The weighted prevalence of depressive symptoms was 6.9%, and that of poor SRH was 22.5%. Compared with contact four or more times per week, family or relative contact less than once per month was associated with depressive symptoms (aOR = 1.50, 95% CI: 1.31–1.72) and poor SRH (aOR = 1.28, 95% CI: 1.17–1.41). Corresponding associations for infrequent friend contact were stronger (aOR = 2.02, 95% CI: 1.75–2.34; aOR = 1.77, 95% CI: 1.63–1.93, respectively). Lack of neighborhood trust was also associated with both outcomes. These findings suggest that specific social relationships, particularly friendships, are relevant to mental and perceived health among adults living alone.

paper_title: Humanize Olympiad Agents: A Multi-Session Workflow for Olympiad Problem Solving with Solve, Review, Wiki, Verify
paper_abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly improving on long-horizon scientific and olympiad tasks. Recent systems have produced a Lean-formalized resolution of the Navier--Stokes problem and autonomous solutions to four open questions in the Erdős Conjectures database. Yet neither system releases both its underlying model and complete inference stack. More broadly, a single agent session remains brittle on difficult problems: early errors can propagate, missing domain knowledge can stall progress, and apparent success can mask a misinterpretation or weakening of the original task. We introduce HOA (Humanize Olympiads Agent), an open, flow-level framework that coordinates multiple agent sessions through three complementary feedback channels. First, an independent reviewer evaluates each candidate and provides actionable feedback. Second, a structured wiki supplies task-specific knowledge that may be missing or unreliable in model pretraining. Third, a verifier checks generated Lean proofs against trusted challenge statements. With GPT-5.6 Sol, HOA achieves perfect scores on the IMO, IPhO, and IOI 2026, near-full marks on the IChO 2026 problem set, and solves all 672 problems (100%) on PutnamBench. On the Lean-Eval leaderboard, HOA ranks first, solving 251 of 304 problems (82.6%). We further evaluate HOA with open models. Using Kimi-K3, HOA achieves full scores on the IMO, IPhO, and IOI, and a gold-level score of 97.1% on the IChO. These results closely match the closed-source GPT-5.6 Sol + /Goal baseline on the IMO and IPhO, while exceeding it on the IChO and IOI, demonstrating that systematic feedback can help bridge substantial differences in base-model capability.

paper_title: From Cell Chemistry to Combat Power: A Mission-Driven Review of Battery-Dependent and Electrically Powered Military Systems
paper_abstract: Military capability increasingly depends on electrical energy for sensing, communications, computing, autonomy, mobility, protection, electronic warfare, and electrically enabled weapons. However, the value of a battery or energy-storage technology cannot be judged from chemistry or cell-level energy density alone. This review develops a mission-driven framework linking cell chemistry → module/pack → power electronics and thermal management → platform integration → mission effect → operational energy and contested logistics. It distinguishes energy from power and organizes military systems into four analytical battery roles: battery-integral, battery-dependent, battery-buffered, and battery-secondary. The framework is applied across soldier systems, smart munitions, unmanned systems, tactical vehicles, naval platforms, and high-power electrically enabled systems. The review finds that no universal “best military battery” exists; technology selection must reflect mission duty cycle, power demand, environmental exposure, survivability, recharge or resupply conditions, and system integration. Cell-level advantages can be reduced by pack overhead, protection, thermal management, power conversion, degradation, maintainability, and logistics. The review also proposes a cross-level evidence framework that distinguishes cell, pack, platform, modeled, demonstrated, operational, and fielded evidence. These findings support a mission-driven transition roadmap and strategic implications for force design, acquisition, research priorities, and operational-energy planning.

paper_title: Vesicular Protocells at the Origin of Life: A Critical Review and a Bounded Bio-Inspired Analogy
paper_abstract: Membrane-bounded vesicles assembled from prebiotically plausible amphiphiles remain one of the most experimentally supported models of early compartmentalization. Mixed single-chain amphiphiles form vesicles over a wider pH and salinity range than early single-component fatty-acid systems; such vesicles can grow, divide by physically or chemically simple routes, and, in selected formulations, host limited nonenzymatic nucleic-acid chemistry. This article reviews those results, with emphasis on work since the 2018 syntheses of Joyce and Szostak and of Chen and Walde, and separates them from a second, independent question: whether modern microbial biofilms can be used as functional analogs when thinking about matrix-stabilized compartments.The two questions are independent in claim-type and must not be fused, but they are linked by an explicit translation rule. Extracellular polymeric substances, short-chain fatty acids, and other products of evolved metabolism are not demonstrated prebiotic building blocks. A publicly posted preprint by the present author coupled a vesicular framework to microbial-biofilm language [20]. Preliminary morphological observations of heat-treated probiotic biofilms after rehydration, developed in drafts leading to that preprint, do not establish a vesicle-to-cell transition, do not document sterility, and cannot be read as abiogenesis. Even a later, well-controlled demonstration of survival after autoclaving would concern persistence of pre-existing biological material, not the emergence of cells from nonliving chemistry. An informal coupling of pH gradients to zeta potential is retained only as a qualitative analogy that currently lacks defined variables, energy accounting, kinetics, and falsifying predictions.The recommended path is therefore split in its inferences and joined in its constraints: a microbiological study of matrix-protected survival, if pursued at all, should meet sterilization-validation standards and remain silent on origin-of-life claims; protocell experiments should start from abiotic amphiphile mixtures and specified geochemical boundary conditions, and should obey the same translation rules used to reject the biofilm reading. Within those limits, vesicular models continue to offer a coherent experimental program for the chemistry-to-biology transition.

paper_title: Urban Region Representation Learning: A Survey of Data, Methodological Families, Applications, and Evaluation
paper_abstract: Urban computing increasingly relies on representations of bounded areas such as neighborhoods, census tracts, and traffic-analysis zones. Urban Region Representation Learning (URRL) transforms heterogeneous spatial-structural data, human mobility, POIs and urban text, urban imagery, and societal or environmental evidence into reusable region representations for functional inference, socioeconomic estimation, mobility and demand prediction, and emerging urban reasoning tasks. The URRL literature spans statistical context and spatial-smoothness modeling, graph-based relational learning, contrastive and self-supervised alignment, and foundation-model-based knowledge transfer and task adaptation. Although existing surveys provide valuable perspectives on urban data fusion and broad geospatial representation learning, they do not jointly examine the region as the learned unit, the hybrid composition of modern URRL systems, and the comparability of their evaluation protocols. To address this gap, we review URRL through an integrated data-method-application-evaluation framework. We examine how urban evidence is aggregated to regions and constrained by scale, vintage, coverage, and measurement bias. We then organize representative methods into four dominant, non-exclusive families and use inductive bias to interpret their representation mechanisms, learning signals, and imported knowledge. Finally, we synthesize applications and develop a protocol-aware evaluation framework that distinguishes resources, experimental configurations, and public benchmarks, while separating within-city reuse from geographic, partition, temporal, and missing-evidence generalization.

paper_title: Prismatic Image Relocation in Macular Disease: Effects on Visual Function and the Preferred Retinal Locus-A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
paper_abstract: Purpose: To evaluate the effectiveness of prismatic image relocation for visual rehabilitation in patients with macular disease and central vision loss, focusing on visual acuity, reading-related outcomes, preferred retinal locus (PRL) behaviour, fixation, and functional outcomes. Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 and prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261500738). Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, PubMed/MEDLINE, and CENTRAL were searched from inception to September 2026. Randomized, non-randomized comparative, pre-post, and case-series studies evaluating prism-based image relocation were eligible. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2, ROBINS-I, or the appropriate Joanna Briggs Institute tools. Random-effects meta-analysis was performed when studies were sufficiently comparable. Results: Eleven studies met the inclusion criteria. Two randomized controlled trials provided comparable data for the primary meta-analysis of distance visual acuity. The pooled point estimate was in the direction of better visual acuity with prism correction but was imprecise and included the null effect (MD, −0.218 logMAR; 95% CI, −0.522 to 0.086), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 94.5%). The certainty of evidence for the primary outcome was rated as very low. Sensitivity analyses did not materially strengthen the evidence. Observational studies frequently reported favourable visual or functional outcomes, but several were affected by important risks of selection bias, confounding, or absence of appropriate control groups. Conclusions: The available evidence indicates that prismatic image relocation can modify retinal image position and may provide visual or functional benefit in selected patients with central vision loss, although the certainty of evidence regarding its effect on distance visual acuity is very low.

paper_title: Genetic Engineering and Evolution Across Biological Systems: A Structured Review of the Origin, Transmission, and Population Fate of Engineered Variation
paper_abstract: Genetic engineering deliberately alters biological material, but the transmission, spread, and continued function of engineered variation remain subject to evolutionary processes. This structured narrative review compares engineered crops, insect gene drives, and engineered microbes through an origin–transmission–population fate framework, distinguishing control at the sequence, inheritance, and ecological levels. Crop studies document pollen-mediated gene flow, multi-year transgene persistence in a weedy relative, and pest resistance alongside regional pest suppression. Gene-drive studies demonstrate biased inheritance and collapse of particular cage populations, while resistance and ecological heterogeneity constrain extrapolation to other settings. Microbial studies show that construct burden, genetic exchange, and selection can undermine intended functions despite successful initial engineering and host colonization. Together, these findings distinguish molecular precision from control over inheritance, population persistence, and ecological outcomes: initial technical success does not establish lasting practical benefit. The review maps research designs to the claims they can support and identifies difficulties in comparison across systems, interpretation of evidence, and observation over relevant evolutionary time scales. Priorities include multigenerational monitoring, comparable measures of genetic persistence and functional stability, and staged, context-sensitive evaluation. The framework connects molecular intervention with population processes and clarifies the evidence needed for biosafety and governance decisions.

paper_title: A Design-Based Mood’s Median Test for Complex Survey Data
paper_abstract: Comparing central tendency across groups in complex survey data is challenging when outcome variables are skewed or contain outliers. While Mood’s median test provides a robust nonparametric solution under simple random sampling, it is not directly applicable to data arising from complex survey designs. This article proposes a design-based extension that integrates weighted median estimation with Rao–Scott adjusted tests of independence.The method replaces sample counts with estimated population totals derived from survey weights and uses design-consistent variance estimation to account for clustering, stratification, and unequal probabilities of selection. A Rao–Scott correction is then applied to obtain valid inference. The approach is demonstrated using data from a WHO STEPS survey, highlighting its practical utility in epidemiological applications.

paper_title: Geographic Variations in the Clinical and Hematological Manifestations of Pediatric Visceral Leishmaniasis: A Systematic Review
paper_abstract: Background: Visceral leishmaniasis (VL), or kala-azar, is one of the most devastating neglected tropical diseases, disproportionately affecting children in resource-limited endemic regions across four major geographic zones. Despite decades of research, no comprehensive systematic review has rigorously compared clinical and hematological manifestations of pediatric VL across these regions, leaving clinicians without evidence-based, region-specific guidelines. Objectives: To analyze and compare the clinical, hematological, and epidemiological patterns of pediatric VL across four major endemic regions: Mediterranean/Europe, Latin America, East/Central Africa, and Asia (West, Central, and East). Secondary objectives included comparing parasite species distributions, diagnostic approaches, treatment regimens, complication profiles, and case-fatality rates. Methods: A systematic literature search following PRISMA 2020 guidelines and PRISMA-S reporting standards was conducted across Pub-Med/MEDLINE, Scopus, ISI Web of Science, EMBASE, and CINAHL. The review protocol was retrospectively registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; Registration No.: CRD420261446750). Retrospective PROSPERO registration is acknowledged as a limitation of this review. Duplicate records were removed using Rayyan software. From 1,482 identified records, after removing 117 duplicates and applying pre-specified inclusion/exclusion criteria, 40 studies met all eligibility criteria: Mediterranean/Europe (n=13), Latin America (n=6), East/Central Africa (n=6), and Asia (n=15). Study quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Checklist. Cross-tabulations were performed for exploratory descriptive purposes; results are presented as narative synthesis. Results: Apparent geographic variations were observed. Fever was near-universal (91-100%) across all regions. Splenomegaly ranged from 90% to 98%, and hepatomegaly from 65% to 89%. Anemia prevalence ranged from 78% to 95%, pancytopenia from 45% to 72%, and thrombocytopenia from 62% to 92% (based on exploratory cross-tabulations). Leishmania infantum predominated in Mediterranean/European and Latin American regions; L. donovani prevailed in African and Asian cohorts. Treatment regimens, diagnostic methods, and complication profiles showed substantial regional differences. Conclusions: Apparent geographic variations exist in pediatric VL manifestations, which may be associated with differences in parasite species, host genetics, nutritional status, healthcare infrastructure, and co-infection patterns. Region-specific diagnostic and therapeutic guidelines are urgently needed and should be supported by enhanced surveillance and collaborative international research.

paper_title: Clinical Applications of Metabolomics in Paediatric Brain Tumours and Other Solid Tumours: A Review
paper_abstract: There is growing interest in utilising metabolomics as a tool in childhood cancer research. We propose four main applications of metabolomics in this context; as a less invasive diagnostic technique, to identify prognostic biomarkers, to monitor disease progression or detect relapse and to identify novel therapeutic targets. MEDLINE, PubMed, EMBASE and Cochrane databases were searched. Studies evaluating metabolomics in paediatric brain and other solid tumours in the context of our four applications were included. Studies evaluating other ‘omics’ modalities, tumour types, outcomes or involving adults were excluded. 39 articles were included. Published evidence in brain tumours includes the potential for metabolomics to identify biomarkers from peripheral blood samples, possibly obviating the need for invasive biopsies. Additionally, magnetic resonance spectroscopy adds value to conventional magnetic resonance imaging for diagnosis and prognostication. Considering other solid tumours, metabolomics has been evaluated in neuroblastoma for risk stratification of disease and in osteosarcoma, retinoblastoma, Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma for identifying novel diagnostic biomarkers and improving understanding of tumour pathophysiology. Our review highlights the wide-ranging applications of metabolomics across paediatric brain and other solid tumours. There is an emerging role for metabolomics within research and clinical spheres to improve the diagnosis and management of childhood cancers.

paper_title: Review of Power Management Integrated Circuits for Energy Harvesting
paper_abstract: This manuscript presents a review of Power Management Integrated Circuits (PMICs) for energy harvesting applications, covering both commercial off-the-shelf components and academic custom designs reported between 2014 and mid-2026. A two-round search across seven databases processed 1393 sources, of which 102 met the inclusion criteria after deduplication and screening. The review addresses the principal harvesting modalities considered in the literature surveyed, that is, solar/photovoltaic, thermoelectric, piezoelectric, radio-frequency, and hybrid/multisource systems, and examines commercial PMICs alongside state-of-the-art academic prototypes, including designs reported at ISSCC 2025 and ISSCC 2026 conferences. Real-world deployment cases with measured results are analyzed across five application domains: IoT sensor nodes, wearable and implantable devices, structural health monitoring, UAV energy harvesting, and unconventional sources. Key performance metrics are compared, including quiescent current, cold-start voltage, minimum operating voltage, conversion efficiency, and MPPT performance. Academic designs have demonstrated quiescent currents as low as 32 nA, cold-start operation at 57 mV, sustained converter operation from 3.5 mV after startup, and MPPT efficiencies exceeding 99%. Controlled comparisons of commercial PMICs show that their relative performance depends strongly on source impedance, voltage level, excitation conditions, and startup requirements; accordingly, a first-pass selection procedure organized by operating regime is proposed. Five trends shaping next-generation PMICs are identified: inductorless charge-pump architectures, batteryless intermittent-computing integration, TinyML on harvested energy, multi-source chip-level integration, and advanced CMOS integration, represented in the surveyed literature by implementations down to 28 nm FDSOI. The review concludes that the commercial–academic performance gap has narrowed substantially for quiescent current, conversion efficiency, and MPPT performance, whereas custom circuits retain a clear advantage in ultra-low-voltage startup and sustained operation for thermoelectric harvesting.

paper_title: Prolonged Extremity Tourniquet Use in Wilderness and Austere Trauma: A Rapid Review and Exploratory Meta-Analysis
paper_abstract: Background: Extremity tourniquets are established lifesaving interventions for severe traumatic hemorrhage, but much of the supporting evidence comes from systems in which evacuation and surgical care occur rapidly. Wilderness, rural, disaster, and contemporary battlefield environments may expose patients to substantially longer tourniquet times. This review examined duration-related outcomes of prolonged emergency tourniquet use and the implications for delayed evacuation. Methods: A rapid review was performed using PubMed/MEDLINE, Google Scholar, backward citation searching, and relevant wilderness and military guidance through Aug 6, 2026. Human trauma studies reporting tourniquet duration and clinical outcomes were eligible. Primary prolonged-use cohorts were included in an exploratory random-effects meta-analysis of amputation proportion. Prolonged use was defined as more than 120 minutes for the primary synthesis; a sensitivity analysis was restricted to cohorts with tourniquet duration greater than 4 hours. Results: Three primary prolonged-use cohorts provided extractable patient-level amputation data (105 patients). The pooled amputation proportion was 35.3% (95% CI, 26.8%-44.9%; I2=0%). Restriction to the two cohorts with tourniquet duration greater than 4 hours produced a similar estimate of 34.9% (95% CI, 25.8%-45.2%). Prolonged cohorts also reported substantial rates of nerve injury, infection, acute kidney injury, rhabdomyolysis, dialysis, and compartment syndrome. In contrast, military and civilian studies dominated by shorter application times reported low tourniquet-attributable morbidity and substantial hemorrhage-control benefit. Conclusions: Emergency tourniquets remain appropriate for life-threatening extremity hemorrhage, but the risk profile changes as evacuation time lengthens. The available evidence supports aggressive reassessment and, when trained personnel and appropriate conditions are present, timely conversion to another effective hemorrhage-control method before ischemic exposure becomes prolonged. Beyond approximately 6 hours, reperfusion and release become higher-risk decisions that should occur with advanced monitoring and resuscitative capability whenever possible. The certainty of evidence is low because prolonged-use studies are small, retrospective, and strongly confounded by injury severity.

paper_title: AI-Based Methods for Geomechanical Containment-Risk Assessment in Geological CO₂ Storage: A Systematic Review
paper_abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used to support the assessment of geomechanical containment risk in geological CO₂ storage; however, the suitability of different model families remains strongly dependent on the task, data representation, and target variable. This systematic review followed PRISMA 2020 and analyzed 63 studies published between 2021 and 2026, identified through IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and Scopus. The evidence was synthesized according to AI family, application, inputs, outputs, dataset origin, validation strategy, predictive performance, computational efficiency, and relationship with geomechanical containment risk. CNN/U-Net, FFNN/MLP/DNN, and conventional machine-learning methods were the most frequently used families, while FNO, recurrent models, GNN, PINN, GAN/cGAN, and reduced-order approaches addressed more specialized spatial, temporal, physical, and optimization tasks. Only 17 studies (27%) predicted at least one direct geomechanical response or risk indicator, whereas 42 studies (66.7%) relied exclusively on synthetic or simulation-generated data. AI surrogates consistently reduced computational cost, enabling rapid scenario evaluation and optimization, but field validation of directly geomechanical models remained limited. Overall, no universally superior architecture was identified; model suitability is task-dependent. Future progress requires hybrid datasets, external field validation, uncertainty quantification, and reproducible workflows integrating AI with multiphysics simulation and monitoring data.

paper_title: How Do Energy Shocks Affect Financial Markets: Systematic Literature Review
paper_abstract: This paper applies the systematic literature review (SLR) method to examine the effects of energy shocks on financial markets in the academic literature. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, the study uses the Scopus database to identify relevant articles published between 2022 and 2026. From 710 initial records, 109 articles were selected after applying predefined eligibility and screening criteria. The literature covers stock, foreign exchange, bond and green financial markets, as well as multi-market and broader macro-financial effects. The findings show that energy shocks affect financial markets through heterogeneous, asymmetric and time-varying mechanisms. Their effects depend on the type of shock, market characteristics, country-specific factors and prevailing economic conditions. Supply, demand and risk shocks generate different responses, while spillovers tend to increase during periods of uncertainty and financial stress. The review highlights the importance of energy shocks as a source of financial market volatility and their influence on financial conditions through economic activity, inflation, credit conditions and expectations.

paper_title: From Detecting Drift to Adapting to It: A Critical Review of Hybrid Drift-Aware IoT Intrusion Detection and a Stacked Adaptive Ensemble Framework for TON_IoT
paper_abstract: Machine-learning intrusion detection for the Internet of Things (IoT) is increasingly judged on whether it survives changing traffic, not only on benchmark accuracy. This review appraises one recent response, the hybrid Random Forest (RF), benign-only Isolation Forest (IF) and Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) drift-monitoring framework of Obaidat, Abouali and Shakeel (2026), and uses the appraisal to specify a fused, adaptive alternative. Working only from the confusion matrix and tables the authors publish, we derive a Matthews correlation coefficient of about 0.94 and a benign-class F1 of about 0.94, show that the hybrid raises about 158 more false alarms than RF with no visible recall gain, and show that its advantage on an unseen attack family (85.26% versus 85.18% on 4,952 flows) lies well inside sampling error. We then compare 13 stacking, adaptive and multi-stage studies from 2023–2026 and find, within the sources read, none that combines trained stacking, automatic drift adaptation and evaluation on TON_IoT. We present EHAE-IDS: RF, Gradient Boosting and an online Adaptive Random Forest as Level-0 learners, a Logistic Regression meta-learner, an ADWIN-gated and validated update loop, and a two-stage binary-then-multiclass detector, together with a four-protocol evaluation plan with controlled drift injection, label-delay scenarios, edge-cost metrics and statistical testing. No experimental results are reported. The paper is a review and a pre-specified design, and its expected-outcome section states hypotheses and how each could fail.

paper_title: Minimal Literature Assessment Norms (MiLAN) for Medical and Public Health Reviews
paper_abstract: This article proposes a set of criteria that establish normative checkpoints essential for producing literature reviews beyond those focused on intervention effects (e.g., Cochrane, PRISMA) or observational studies (e.g., STROBE). Our proposed framework, which we refer to as minimal literature assessment norms (MiLAN), is intended to enhance the rigor and value of traditional narrative reviews. MiLAN outlines three core methodological processes that should be described in a manuscript’s methods section: search, selection, and presentation. By articulating these minimum expectations, MiLAN aims to increase transparency and reproducibility in narrative review methodologies while preserving the adaptability that makes narrative reviews valuable. This approach allows authors whose topics, goals, or resources do not align with the demands of complex systematic review frameworks to still present their work in a clear, accountable, and methodologically sound manner.

paper_title: Quantum Machine Learning and Quantum-Assisted Artificial Intelligence Applications in Orthopedics and Medicine: A Systematic Review
paper_abstract: Background and Objectives: Quantum machine learning (QML) leverages quantum computing principles to enhance artificial intelligence applications in health care. We aimed to conduct a systematic literature review following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 guidelines to evaluate QML and quantum-assisted artificial intelligence (AI) applications in orthopedics and medicine.Materials and Methods: Comprehensive searches were performed across SciSpace, Google Scholar, and PubMed, yielding 1,068 initial records. After deduplication (819 unique records), abstract screening (threshold ≥4.0), and full-text screening (threshold ≥4.5), 97 studies met the inclusion criteria. Screening criteria included medical and orthopedic application, quantum-enhanced AI intervention, comparative performance evaluation, and clinical/computational outcome reporting. Data extraction focused on study design, quantum ML methods, medical application domains, key findings, performance comparisons, and clinical implications. Prediction model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST) guidelines were used to assess risk of the studies that report superior performance of QML over conventional ML or others.Results: The 97 included studies demonstrated diverse applications of QML across multiple medical domains, including orthopedics, oncology, cardiology, neurology, ophthalmology, and other specialties. Quantum approaches included quantum neural networks, quantum support vector machines, variational quantum classifiers, hybrid quantum-classical models, quantum transfer learning, and quantum federated learning. Performance comparisons consistently showed quantum-enhanced methods achieving comparable or superior accuracy to classical approaches. The overall risk of bias for all 11 studies with superior performance was determined as high risk using PROBAST guidelines.Conclusions: QML demonstrates significant promise for enhancing diagnostic accuracy, treatment optimization, and predictive analytics in orthopedics and medicine. Although current implementations face challenges related to hardware limitations, scalability, and clinical validation requirements, the evidence suggests that hybrid quantum-classical approaches offer practical pathways toward clinical adoption with the awareness of reports with high risk of bias. Future studies should focus on large-scale clinical trials and real-world validation of QML.

paper_title: Demand Promotion Interventions to Improve COVID-19 Vaccine Uptake: A Systematic Review of the Global Evidence
paper_abstract: Background/Objectives: The global rollout of COVID-19 vaccines faced significant implementation challenges: limited adult immunization infrastructure, particularly in low- and middle-income countries; rapidly shifting viral epidemiology driven by emerging variants; and widespread vaccine misinformation that fueled hesitancy. Achieving the high coverage necessary to curb transmission required urgent attention to demand-side barriers, making the identification of effective interventions a critical public health priority. This systematic review synthesized global evidence on communication, behavioral, and health systems interventions to increase COVID-19 vaccine demand and uptake. The review assessed intervention effectiveness across diverse population groups and settings and identified lessons to inform the design of adult vaccination programs and future outbreak response. Methods: Between March 2022 and July 2024, we performed a systematic search in PubMed, Scopus, and Global Index Medicus, for COVID-19 demand and uptake studies published after December 2020, with no language or geographic restrictions. Eligible papers were those that reported intervention studies with quantitative comparative outcomes on vaccination attitudes, appointment rates, uptake, or coverage following an intervention. Study quality was assessed using adapted Critical Appraisal Skills Program (CASP) criteria. Studies were categorized into nine intervention approaches, based on an adapted communication and service-delivery taxonomy. Interventions operated at individual, systems, and structural levels. A narrative synthesis was combined with vote counting of studies with positive findings to understand what intervention approaches were effective. and under what conditions. Results: From over 23,000 records, 57 studies from 27 countries met inclusion and quality criteria. Most studies were conducted in high-income countries. Overall, 70% of studies reported positive findings on at least one vaccination outcome. Educational interventions were the most frequently studied approach and were most effective when delivered through multiple channels by trusted messengers and integrated with complementary strategies, rather than as standalone information provision. Reminder and nudge interventions showed mixed results, performing best when embedded within multicomponent approaches that addressed both logistical and attitudinal barriers. Access-enhancing and service delivery interventions demonstrated the most consistent evidence of effectiveness, with nine of ten studies reporting positive outcomes; successful approaches included on-site vaccination, mobile units, pharmacy and community health worker delivery, and integration into existing healthcare touchpoints. Vaccine mandates demonstrated the strongest and most consistent effects on coverage at scale, though their coercive mechanism raises ethical considerations around autonomy, equity, and public trust. Conclusions: Improving COVID-19 vaccine uptake requires interventions that simultaneously address knowledge gaps, practical barriers to access, and structural determinants of vaccination behavior. The most effective strategies combined educational, behavioral, and service delivery components tailored to the needs and barriers of specific groups. Policymakers should prioritize access-enhancing and systems-strengthening interventions as a foundation, supplement these with targeted communication delivered by trusted messengers, and reserve mandate-based approaches for situations where less restrictive measures have proven insufficient. These findings have relevance beyond COVID-19, offering transferable lessons for adult immunization programs and future outbreak preparedness.

paper_title: Beyond QAOA: A Review of AI and Quantum Computing for Adaptive Combinatorial Optimization
paper_abstract: Near-term quantum approaches to combinatorial optimization are limited by qubit counts, circuit fidelity, sampling cost, and the difficulty of encoding constraints, while machine learning is increasingly used to configure and control quantum optimization workflows. We call such workflows adaptive: decisions conventionally fixed in advance, from formulation and penalties to shot budgets, backends, and whether to invoke a quantum processor at all, are made by learned policies that respond to the instance, the progress of the solve, or the hardware. This review examines three paradigms, AI for quantum optimization, quantum for AI-driven optimization, and AI-quantum co-optimization, and organizes the literature by the decision being learned rather than by application. A structured search identified a 119-paper corpus, of which 67 papers form an evidence core coded in detail. The evidence is considerably stronger for AI-assisted quantum optimization than for the reverse direction: learning already reduces quantum evaluations, improves initialization, supports decomposition and penalty control, and mitigates noise, whereas evidence that quantum computation improves learned optimizers remains largely confined to small-scale simulation. Experimental controls are thin: of 52 studies in the three paradigms, 22 include no classical baseline, the quantum contribution is fully isolated in 10 of 24 where an ablation applies, and the median largest experiment uses 16 qubits. We introduce an M0-M5 evidence hierarchy, from simulation to practical quantum advantage, and find no broadly convincing result at the highest level. We argue that scaling is increasingly a systems problem: the question is not only whether a problem fits on a quantum processor, but how classical and quantum resources should be allocated across the optimization process.
comments: 36 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables; supplementary evidence matrix included as ancillary file. v2: clarified terminologies, co-optimization definition and evidence denominators; added references, minor corrections

paper_title: How Is Automated Research Evaluated? A Survey of Benchmarks and Evaluation Practices
paper_abstract: Automated research systems support literature synthesis, ideation, experiments, writing, and peer review, but their evaluation is dispersed across tasks, benchmarks, and studies that are difficult to compare directly. We review this literature from the perspective of evaluation design and evidence, covering six targets: literature synthesis, research ideation, executable workflows, scholarly writing and communication, automatic peer review, and end-to-end research. We compare task construction, evidence sources, evaluators, and scoring procedures to explain the capabilities assessed by different designs. Our synthesis highlights three recurring lessons: output checks, process checks, and human studies provide complementary information; evaluator calibration is specific to the property being assessed; and resource budgets and attempt selection are integral to interpreting performance comparisons. We identify diagnostic evaluation designs and documented gaps in supporting evidence, and translate these comparisons into reporting and audit recommendations for specific evaluation settings. The survey helps readers navigate existing evaluations, select appropriate benchmarks, and design subsequent studies.

paper_title: What Output-Only Review Cannot Verify: Study Contracts for Research Agents
paper_abstract: Some defects in an AI-generated study can be identified from its artifacts; others require knowledge of what was approved before execution. We propose study contracts that bind declared experimental choices, run obligations and claim scope to recorded execution evidence, and distinguish this contract-relative verification from scientific truth. A diagnostic using eight self-authored clean/mutated pairs illustrates the information boundary. A deterministic checker applying a registered, fault-specific rule to approved and executed objects detected all eight registered mutations. Across eighteen recorded judge aliases given individual metadata-filtered packages without pair context or the registry-selected fault label, 104 of 144 mutated evaluation cases received defect flags; the remaining cases comprised 32 abstentions and eight terminal failures, with no explicit clean decisions on mutated cases. Some packages retained approval and execution fields, including digests. The prompt instructed judges to abstain when evidence was insufficient. These results characterize a deliberately information-asymmetric development setting; they do not isolate the effect of authoritative information from differences in task specification and rule selection, and they are not comparative verifier quality or agent reward hacking. We identify full-information comparisons, legitimate-adaptation controls and closed-loop agent evaluations as necessary tests of whether contract checks improve useful compliant completion under optimization.
comments: 15 pages, 4 tables. Preprint. Not peer reviewed. Companion manuscripts prepared in parallel

paper_title: Writing for the Reviewer: Defensive Writing in GPT Models
paper_abstract: Researchers increasingly use ChatGPT to revise their papers, and recent GPT versions often narrow or even retract the authors' claims. We call such changes defensive writing when the given material does not support them, and we test two explanations: the model corrects the authors' overclaiming, or it writes for an anticipated reviewer. We ask GPT versions and models from other developers to rewrite paragraphs from papers written before ChatGPT, or to write from an evidence sheet that lists a paper's method and results. Defensive writing grows with GPT version. GPT-6-astra retracts the authors' claims outright, and when it writes from the evidence sheet, it still adds the most ungrounded qualifications. The results favor the anticipated-review explanation, and correcting overclaiming explains only a small part. When the models are only asked to polish, defense stays near the level of the originals; mentioning review raises it, and one round of self-review raises it further. At the same time, fewer than one in ten of the claims GPT-6-astra retracts are overstated. AI reviewers score defensive rewrites higher, while human readers find them harder to read and the authors less certain. Combining AI writing with AI review may amplify this style.

paper_title: Multimodal Remote Sensing Image Registration: A Comprehensive Review, Challenges and Prospects
paper_abstract: Multimodal remote sensing image registration is a crucial prerequisite for the collaborative processing and downstream application of remote sensing data, such as image fusion, change detection, and target recognition. However, significant variations in radiometry, geometry, scale, viewpoint, and time often exist between multimodal images. These differences, driven by varying sensor geometries, physical radiation mechanisms, imaging platforms, and environmental disturbances, pose severe challenges to achieving high-precision, robust registration. This paper systematically reviews the progress of mainstream multimodal remote sensing image registration methods. Based on their registration pipelines, existing approaches are categorized into three main types: region-based, feature-based, and deep learning-based methods. We detail the core principles, representative algorithms, advantages, and limitations of each category. Additionally, we summarize publicly available multimodal image datasets in the remote sensing domain, analyzing their specific characteristics and applicable scenarios. Finally, we highlight current bottlenecks in high-precision registration research and outline future development trends. This review aims to provide a comprehensive reference and valuable insights for researchers in related fields.
comments: 12 figures, 8 tables, 135 references. Review article accepted for publication in Photogrammetric Engineering and Remote Sensing (ASPS), manuscript number PERS-26-00034

paper_title: Beyond Imitation: A Framework and Benchmark for LLM-Assisted Peer Review
paper_abstract: The rapid growth of scientific publishing has strained peer review, particularly in machine learning, raising concerns about declining review quality and increasing reviewer workload. Large language models (LLMs) have been proposed as automated review assistants, yet their evaluation has focused largely on imitating human-written reviews rather than supporting the core functions of peer review. Here, we introduce a verification-centric perspective on LLM-assisted peer review, emphasizing error detection as a critical and resource-intensive task. We present a scalable benchmark that evaluates review systems' ability to identify logical contradictions, constructed through synthetic insertion of errors into conference papers, yielding unambiguous evaluation targets and enabling systematic comparison. We further propose a Multi-Layered Review (MLR) framework that prioritizes detailed manuscript comprehension before review generation, aligning more closely with human reviewing practices while improving token efficiency. Across evaluations, our approach demonstrates strong alignment with human review scores, achieves high error detection performance, and provides complementary perspectives on reviewer focus. These improvements can be attributed to both the choice of the underlying LLM and the design of our system. At the same time, we corroborate persistent vulnerabilities to adversarial manipulation, underscoring the need for robustness in automated review systems. Our findings highlight the importance of rigorous, error-focused evaluation to guide responsible deployment of LLM-based tools in peer review and other critical scientific workflows.

paper_title: Open Science Society: A Scalable and Decentralized Framework for Fraud-Resistant Peer Review
paper_abstract: Traditional scientific publishing and bibliometric models face severe limitations regarding prolonged operational processing times, institutional costs, and vulnerability to systemic evaluation biases. To address these inefficiencies, this paper introduces the Open Science Society (OSS), a scalable, decentralized methodology designed for trusted, fraud-resistant scientific curation and real-time peer-evaluation. Moving away from static, global metric indices and opaque review architectures, the proposed framework implements an endogenous, dynamic evaluation method that calibrates reviewer authority scores based on specialized expertise. Crucially, the methodology computes continuous evaluation weights by projecting domain-specific interaction histories onto a keyword-driven semantic space via a symmetric correlation matrix. Through rigorous mathematical formalization and empirical simulation, we demonstrate that the OSS pipeline effectively isolates strategic manipulation, collapsing the voting weight of unqualified actors or collusive networks to absolute zero while preserving genuine cross-domain authority. The system achieves fast, stationary score convergence, establishing a sustainable algorithmic blueprint to ensure long-term publishing integrity and decentralized bibliometric governance without centralized gatekeepers.

paper_title: Durability and Truck-Loading Vulnerability of Bailey Bridges: A Short Review of Historical Loading, Collapse Cases, and Maintenance Needs
paper_abstract: Bailey bridges were developed as rapidly deployable modular steel bridges, but many have remained in service for decades under traffic and environmental conditions substantially different from those prevailing when they were installed. This review examines the relationship between bridge durability, historical and current truck loading, documented collapse cases, common superstructure failure mechanisms, and maintenance requirements, with evidence from South Asia, Africa, and Ethiopia. The reviewed cases indicate that, despite differences in location and service conditions, in-service Bailey bridge failures exhibit common patterns, including excessive deformation, buckling of critical members, connection failure, structural instability, and progressive superstructure collapse under vehicle loading. Overloading is frequently reported as a direct trigger, while corrosion, ageing, inadequate maintenance, flooding, and scour increase structural vulnerability. In Ethiopia, several old Bailey bridges at different locations experienced in-service collapses during 2024, 2025, and 2026, highlighting the need for systematic assessment of ageing bridges and their current loading demands. The main aim of this review is to identify and characterize common failure mechanisms of in-service Bailey bridges, raise awareness of their structural vulnerabilities, and provide a basis for preliminary investigation of old and potentially unreported Bailey bridges in Ethiopia. Construction-stage failures, such as the launching-related instability reported at the Omo Bridge, represent a separate but important failure category that also requires attention. The review therefore emphasizes condition- and load-based safety assessment through systematic inspection, corrosion and deformation monitoring, truck-load control, structural load rating, and timely strengthening, rehabilitation, or replacement.

paper_title: Curriculum Design for Continuing Professional Education Across Forensic Disciplines: A Scoping Review Protocol
paper_abstract: Introduction: Continuing professional education in forensic practice requires curricula that address disciplinary expertise, interpretation, documentation, and communication while remaining responsive to changing professional needs. This scoping review aims to map how continuing professional education curricula are designed, delivered, assessed, evaluated, and quality-assured across forensic disciplines, including their relationship to ongoing professional competence. Accreditation, certification, and governance will be examined in relation to how they shape educational arrangements. Methods: The review will follow Arksey and O’Malley’s five-stage framework, incorporating Levac and colleagues’ refinements and JBI guidance. Reporting will follow PRISMA-ScR and PRISMA-S. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, CINAHL, and APA PsycINFO will be searched from inception to the final search date, with reference-list searching providing additional sources. Inclusion will be restricted to English-language publications without geographical restrictions. Eligible sources will address continuing professional education or competence maintenance among qualified or practicing forensic professionals and provide substantive information on curriculum design or educational assurance. Sources concerning only undergraduate, pre-licensure, entry-to-practice, or initial specialist education will be excluded unless a separable continuing-development component is reported. Two reviewers will independently screen titles, abstracts, and full texts using Covidence, with disagreements resolved through discussion or a third reviewer. A standardized charting form will be piloted on at least five eligible sources; one reviewer will chart each source, and a second will verify all entries. Results and Analysis: Data will be summarized descriptively and synthesized narratively across the following: learning needs assessment; competencies and objectives; curriculum content and structure; teaching and implementation; assessment and feedback; evaluation and revision; and educational quality assurance. Reported outcomes will be mapped to the four Kirkpatrick levels: reaction, learning, behavior, and results. Measurement methods and follow-up periods will be retained to distinguish immediate learning outcomes from retained competence and workplace application. The synthesis will identify shared educational elements, disciplinary variations, accessibility barriers, and reporting or evaluation gaps to inform subsequent curriculum development. Ethics and Dissemination: Ethical approval is not anticipated because the review will analyze published literature without collecting identifiable participant data. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, relevant professional meetings, and curriculum design summaries for educators, practitioners, professional associations, accrediting organizations, and forensic service leaders.

paper_title: Public Data Resources for the 26 August 2026 Nepal Hazard Cascade: A Living Scoping Review and Data Catalogue
paper_abstract: Publicly available data and information relevant and supportive to the 26 August 2026 Langtang Lirung disaster cascade are dispersed across repositories, data portals and other online sources, complicating their identification, assessment and reuse. This study presents a living catalogue (https://evelpidou.nkua.cloud/Nepal-Flood-2026-Catalogue/) of these resources and analyses its first assessed release, archived in Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23034746). The search and charting process, reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR, comprised 74 documented searches through 24 September 2026, followed by the assessment and reviewing that completed on 28 September. The resulting inventory contains 141 resources and 5,883 assets across eight thematic domains. Structured records preserve provenance, geographic and temporal descriptions, access conditions, rights and source limitations, while the WebGIS (https://evelpidou.nkua.cloud/Nepal-Flood-2026/) enables geographic exploration where spatial information is available. Beyond this initial release, planned periodic searches, event-triggered checks, community nominations and versioned updates provide for continued expansion. The contribution is a traceable inventory connecting pre-event baselines, event observations and subsequent analyses to their supporting material, with documented searches and decisions providing a basis for continued maintenance. The catalogue therefore reduces the time and effort required to identify and access relevant data and information, while lowering the risk of overlooking resources that could inform future investigations of the event. Unlike conventional scoping reviews centred on mapping existing studies or datasets, this approach proposes a new type that systematically identifies and evaluates the data and resources available to support future research.

paper_title: Perceived Barriers for Advance Care Planning Among People with Dementia and Family Caregivers: A Systematic Review of Qualitative Studies
paper_abstract: Background: Advance care planning (ACP) enables individuals to communicate values and preferences for future care before decisional capacity is lost. Although ACP is particularly important for people living with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and dementia, engagement remains low, and the mechanisms underlying this gap are not well understood. This qualitative evidence synthesis examined perceived barriers to ACP among people living with dementia and their family caregivers.Methods: Four were searched from database inception to July 1st 2026, for qualitative studies reporting barriers to ACP among people with MCI or dementia and/or family caregivers. Twenty-four studies conducted across ten countries met inclusion criteria. Barrier statements extracted from included studies were analyzed using thematic synthesis, generating 25 codes grouped into descriptive themes and further abstracted into analytical themes representing dementia-specific mechanisms.Results: Two analytical themes were identified: (1) challenges in preserving the person's voice throughout the dementia trajectory, reflecting a shift toward caregiver-mediated decision-making, assumptions about capacity, and delayed ACP initiation; and (2) challenges in maintaining continuity of expressed values and preferences over time, reflecting uncertainty about future care needs and the limitations of one-time ACP conversations. Three contextual barriers, including limited ACP preparedness, insufficient healthcare professional and system support, and sociocultural influences, further shaped engagement. Methodological quality across included studies was high.Conclusion: ACP in dementia is shaped by challenges extending beyond commonly reported general-population barriers. Effective support for this population requires moving beyond one-time, capacity-focused documentation toward ongoing, relationally embedded approaches to communication and values clarification throughout the disease trajectory.

paper_title: AI-Supported Study Abroad: A Review of Emerging Evidence on Affordable Internationalization at Home
paper_abstract: The cost of study abroad has been a barrier to access for a greater number of students. As a high-impact program, alternative access to study abroad should be pressing. Literature considers study abroad and artificial intelligence in isolation of each other; indicating a deeper widening research gap challenging artificial intelligence as not adequately fitted for alternate resource. Review methodology were limited to high-quality academic research databases. The findings revealed that AI has the capacity to expand access to study abroad through state agency support for institutions, and personalized learning. Access can be enhanced when institutions reverse from operating AI as an isolation, but as exploration of study abroad. Advancing AI supported study abroad programs requires greater investment in technological infrastructure and resources.

paper_title: S-Adenosylmethionine and Perioperative Bleeding Risk: A Case of Mohs Postoperative Hematoma and Scoping Review
paper_abstract: Background: Over-the-counter dietary supplements are commonly used by patients undergoing surgical procedures, but their perioperative effects are often incompletely characterized. S-adenosylmethionine (SAMe) is a widely available supplement used for several conditions, yet its potential effects on hemostasis and perioperative bleeding remain poorly understood. Objective: To map the available clinical and mechanistic evidence regarding SAMe, its related metabolic pathways, and potential effects on hemostasis and perioperative bleeding. Methods: We conducted a PRISMA-guided scoping review of PubMed, Google Scholar, Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov. Studies evaluating SAMe or related components of one-carbon metabolism in relation to perioperative bleeding, coagulation, platelet function, endothelial function, or other physiologic pathways relevant to hemostasis were considered. Conclusions: No human clinical evidence directly linking SAMe supplementation to perioperative bleeding was identified. Existing literature provides limited mechanistic evidence that SAMe and related one-carbon metabolic pathways may influence physiologic processes relevant to hemostasis, but these findings do not establish an association with surgical bleeding. Further clinical and mechanistic studies are needed to characterize the perioperative safety of SAMe.

paper_title: Artificial Intelligence for Intraoperative Bleeding Detection: A Narrative Review
paper_abstract: Timely recognition of intraoperative bleeding can support visualization and hemostatic response. This narrative review organizes representative systems by temporal purpose - anticipation, detection, and post-hoc assessment - while treating input sources separately. Video classifiers, object detectors, segmentation-assisted models, and synchronized device - video pipelines demonstrate distinct capabilities, but their reported metrics are not interchangeable. One device-associated detector achieved 81.0% sensitivity with 4.6% precision, corresponding to roughly eight false alerts per operation, whereas other studies evaluated event counts, duration, or warning lead time. We distinguish offline testing, streaming feasibility, and prospective intraoperative evaluation, and relate these evidence levels to event-level accuracy, alert burden, and response time. Current evidence remains limited by small datasets, uncertain transfer across procedures and institutions, workflow integration, and surgeon interaction. Future studies should test transferable contextual cues and determine prospectively whether alerts improve recognition or hemostatic response without excessive interruption.

paper_title: From Passive Perception to Active Interaction: A Survey of Affordance Learning for Embodied AI
paper_abstract: Embodied AI aims to develop agents that perceive, reason, and act in physical environments. Beyond recognizing objects and scenes, agents must identify possible interactions, determine their relevance to the current task and embodiment, and translate them into executable behavior. Affordance learning supports this process by grounding perception in action possibilities and connecting it with task reasoning and control. Existing affordance surveys, however, provide only partial coverage of the field, often focusing on isolated aspects of perception or robotic interaction and lacking a comprehensive view of the full perception–reasoning–action pipeline in embodied intelligence. To bridge this gap, this survey presents a unified framework organized around three complementary roles: affordance perception identifies possible interactions and their locations; affordance reasoning selects opportu-nities relevant to the task, context, and agent state; and affordance-guided action uses affordance representations for planning and policy learning. Within this framework, we develop fine-grained taxonomies, compare representative methods, and trace the field’s progression from passive visual recognition toward action-aware embodied learning. We further organize representative datasets and evaluation protocols and identify open challenges and future directions. Overall, this survey clarifies how affordance learning connects perception, reasoning, and action to support generalizable and physically grounded embodied intelligence.

paper_title: Neural Question Generation: A Survey of Techniques, Question Types, and Applications
paper_abstract: Neural Question Generation (NQG) has emerged as a foundation for educational technologies and automated assessments. In this study, we perform a survey of NQG over its emerging era from 2020 to 2026. To assess a pool of 109 highly relevant research articles, we systematically follow a five-phase identification and filtering approach. Using this analysis, the study proposes an exhaustive taxonomy that classifies the recent advancements in NQG based on question generation methodology, generation type, input modality, datasets, application domain, control objectives, and evaluation metrics. The findings indicate that there is a paradigm shift in NQG methodologies from rule-based and syntactic heuristics to highly advanced and popular Transformer-based methodologies, accounting for 58% of the methodologies. The results also indicate that although multiple-choice questions are the most prevalent question type in NQG methodologies, there is an increasing trend towards the generation of cognitively complex questions. Furthermore, we conclude that NQG approaches suffer from a lack of appropriate evaluation measures as well as an inability to generate questions at the higher cognitive order of Bloom’s Taxonomy.

paper_title: PairAudit: Guiding Human Review with Graph Tokens under Distribution Shift
paper_abstract: Intrusion detectors can confidently misclassify attacks that were not seen during training. Human review can correct these errors, but only a limited number of cases can be checked. Uncertainty-based review may overlook confident errors, while anomaly scores alone do not show whether changing the review plan will correct more errors. We introduce PairAudit to find overlooked errors and improve review under a fixed budget. Its graph tokens capture prediction patterns across connected nodes. Rather than building another predictor through feature aggregation, PairAudit uses unusual relational patterns to uncover potential errors in existing predictions. Human feedback then helps decide whether these findings justify changing review priorities. Experiments across security tasks show that PairAudit corrects more errors on average than uncertainty-based review, including more errors on unseen attacks. These gains account for all review costs and do not require retraining the detector.

paper_title: A Scoping Review and Experimental Study on Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback for Human-Robot Collaboration
paper_abstract: Human-Robot Collaboration (HRC) can facilitate mass customisation in Industry 4.0, with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) representing a promising approach for developing safe AI-based robots. Practical challenges remain regarding safety during AI development, human feedback quality, and bidirectional human-robot adaptation. We conducted a scoping review of RLHF in HRC systems, mapping methods that address these challenges. Following PRISMA guidelines, we screened 199 records and included 20 peer-reviewed publications (2020-2025) spanning multiple HRC domains. To our knowledge, this is the first review focused on the bidirectional, closed-loop design of RLHF. Our review found multiple feedback modalities enabling data collection in various feedback formats. Collected data can be integrated at different stages of AI training, resulting in a multi-step development process. Pilot experiments are commonly used to evaluate HRC systems based on both human and robot metrics. To empirically test a key gap identified in the review, we conducted a between-subjects VR experiment comparing system- and user-initiated feedback on robot proxemic behaviour for safe navigation. Using Bayesian models, we analysed the relation between the collected feedback and safety metrics: psychological safety (post-experiment questionnaire) and physical safety (inverse time-to-collision). Results show that user-initiated feedback captures perceived safety better than system-initiated feedback, indicating that feedback timing directly affects feedback quality. Our review and experiment findings show that RLHF relies on appropriate feedback methods to ensure AI safety in HRC, and future RLHF research should prioritise realistic HRC experiments evaluating the effects of feedback collection methods on relevant human and robot metrics.

paper_title: A Framework for the Systematic Review of ML Assets in AI Registries
paper_abstract: Background: Modern software systems increasingly rely on Machine Learning (ML) assets (i.e., pre-trained models, datasets, benchmarks) for building, evaluating, and integrating ML-based systems. However, current exploration, selection and reuse practices of ML assets are not supported by systematic retrieval methodologies comparable to those used in traditional evidence synthesis. Consequently, in practice, ML asset selection is often presented as a settled design decision, supported by informal justification rather than a traceable, evidence-based, and updatable selection process. Aims: This paper explores how systematic review methods can support ML asset retrieval. In doing so, we aim to make their selection transparent and reproducible, grounded in explicit evidence, and ultimately better suited to its intended use. Method: We analyze established systematic review practices from scientific literature and adapt their phases (i.e., planning, conducting, and documenting) to Artificial Intelligence (AI) registries, treating ML assets as first-class units of analysis. The resulting framework integrates registry-aware search strategies, cross-registry schema alignment, and dependency-driven ML asset exploration. Results: We conceptualize ML asset retrieval as a systematic and reproducible process rather than an ad hoc activity, and propose a framework for structured ML asset discovery. \textbf{Conclusions:} This work illustrates how systematic review principles can be extended beyond scientific literature to support evidence synthesis over evolving AI registries.

paper_title: LLM-Enabled UAV Dispatch: A System-Level Survey and Taxonomy
paper_abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) dispatch is beginning to move beyond isolated path planning and optimization-driven resource allocation toward system-level coordination supported by semantic reasoning and LLM-based interfaces. This survey provides a unified characterization of LLM-enabled UAV dispatch systems that bridges semantic intent, symbolic decision-making, and physical UAV execution. Rather than treating LLMs as standalone add-ons, we conceptualize them as a cross-layer semantic orchestration layer connecting human instructions, external solvers, and distributed control modules. We organize the literature into four representative dispatch paradigms: pipeline dispatch, global assignment dispatch, decentralized agentic dispatch, and divide-and-conquer dispatch. For each paradigm, we analyze its decision logic, system structure, control flow, representative methods, and potential LLM roles. We further examine how LLMs support semantic parsing, retrieval-grounded planning, solver orchestration, local agent reasoning, multi-agent coordination, safety assessment, and human-facing explanation. We discuss the implications of these paradigms for scalability, robustness, coordination burden, and verification requirements, and identify open challenges including latency-aware reasoning, grounding reliability, physical feasibility guarantees, edge deployment, privacy protection, and distributed consistency. This survey provides a system-level taxonomy and design perspective for integrating LLMs into safety-critical UAV dispatch systems.

paper_title: Cross-Provider Review as a Runtime Contract for Coding Agents: A Controlled Pilot and Fault-Injection Study
paper_abstract: Coding agents increasingly share a workstation while drawing on separate providers and subscription allowances. A second agent can inspect a completed answer, but the call spends another pool and may provide no substantive finding. We describe an advisory cross-provider review contract: distinct resource pools, bounded execution, restricted reviewer capabilities, complete input delivery, usable semantic output, explicit failure states and durable per-attempt evidence. In a controlled, agent-authored pilot of 20 paired development turns, eight had a material reviewer finding (95% exact interval 19.1-63.9%). A boundary-condition scan across both reviewer backends reproduced a previously discovered false success on partial input: four truncation levels passed historically and failed after repair. The scan also found and repaired cancellation during process reaping. In real CLI probes, Claude had no writing tools; Codex attempted writes in five of five read-only trials, each write tool failed, and no disposable repository changed. These tests cover specified paths and versions, not field reliability. A preregistered shadow study of metadata-only review allocation accrued 25 formal observations before an exact-runtime regression found a third defect: a reviewer exiting nonzero with a well-formed verdict was counted as complete. Exit status was not recorded per attempt, so exposure cannot be resolved retrospectively. The 25 formal and two pending records remain an audit cohort; the measurement-valid cohort restarted at zero and collection has begun. No gate result is reported.
comments: 11 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Project page: https://openterminalagent.surge.sh/

paper_title: Has LLM Screening Performance Stalled in Software Engineering Systematic Reviews?
paper_abstract: Screening in systematic reviews (SRs) is manual and time-consuming. Prior work has explored large language models (LLMs) for automating this step, but LLMs are evolving rapidly, so earlier performance claims may no longer accurately reflect their screening performance. We used an existing software engineering SR screening benchmark (SESR-Eval) as our data. We also power-sampled a new, smaller dataset (SESR-Eval-Mini) that allows evaluation at lower costs. Using this data, we evaluated eight new LLMs for screening performance. Additionally, we tested different prompts, analyzed LLM agreement in screening decisions and criteria, and examined the effect of refining the inclusion and exclusion criteria on screening performance. The eight new LLMs performed marginally better than the seven old ones: avg. MCC across secondary studies rose from 0.347 to 0.365. Differences between secondary studies are still bigger than between LLMs. Computing the overall screening decision from criterion-level decisions degraded screening performance only slightly. LLMs generally agree with each other in their corresponding screening decisions (mean Gwet's AC1 = 0.830), though certain inclusion and exclusion criteria showed larger disagreement than others. Refining the inclusion and exclusion criteria slightly improved recall and made decisions easier for some LLMs, but overall impacts of criteria refinement were modest. LLMs are not yet ready to replace humans in paper screening and the advantages new, more costly models bring, appear to be very limited. Agent-based approaches, prompt engineering, and further criteria refinement are three potential future research avenues.
comments: 53 pages, four external figures available in the research artifact

paper_title: Ice-Wedge Thermokarst as a Driver of Formation and Evolution of Thermokarst Lakes: A Review and New Conceptual Model for the Continuous Permafrost Zone
paper_abstract: Thermokarst is a leading destructive geomorphic process in permafrost regions, triggered by the melting of ground ice. Ice-wedge thermokarst features, such as thermokarst lakes and drained-lake basins, are the most abundant thermokarst landforms in the Arctic. In this study, we reassess interactions among factors that drive thermokarst development and evaluate the role of ice-wedge systems in thermokarst-lake formation and evolution. We summarize the factors affecting thermokarst and evaluate mechanisms that facilitate thermokarst-lake development in landscapes of the continuous permafrost zone with abundant ice wedges.
